plan: Fuse ONLY the final affine pair of BF16 elementwise multiplications of a native PyTorch-2.4.1 RMSNorm, leaving the entire normalization reduction graph (pow -> mean(-1) -> +BF16(eps) -> rsqrt) in native Torch so autograd for that branch is bit-for-bit native. Step 1 (host, Torch): compute rstd = rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1,keepdim=True) + BF16(eps)) with eps cast to BF16 and every stage kept in BF16; an independent GPU probe confirmed (x*rstd)*weight with this rstd is bitwise equal to native on all three shapes, while the FP32 all-in-one formula is not, so the reduction is deliberately NOT touched. rstd is produced OUTSIDE the custom Function so its gradient flows back through the native pow/mean/rsqrt accumulation and adds to the direct x-gradient. Step 2 (custom torch.autograd.Function over x, rstd, weight): forward runs a 1D-flattened Triton kernel over numel elements with a tail mask; each element loads x[i], rstd[row=i//512] (per-row broadcast), weight[col=i%512], computes the FIRST product t=x*rstd in fp32 then MATERIALIZES BF16 rounding via .to(bfloat16).to(float32) before the SECOND product t*weight, and stores BF16. This exactly reproduces the native two-stage BF16 rounding between the two multiplications. Launch uses num_warps=4 and attempts enable_fp_fusion=False (portable guard against fused multiply-add) with a TypeError fallback for vendors that do not accept the option; correctness does not depend on it because the intervening BF16 cast already prevents any multiply spanning both stages and each stage is a lone product with no add. Backward is left UNFUSED in Torch to guarantee native BF16 operation order: gw=g*weight; g_input=gw*rstd; g_rstd=sum_to_size(gw*x, rstd.shape); g_weight=sum_to_size(g*(x*rstd), weight.shape) — every elementary product and reduction in native BF16 order and dtype. Input/weight grad dtypes, state_dict, and shapes are unchanged; no tensor is mutated; input may be made contiguous (value- and gradient-preserving) for the flattened kernel. Guards accept only BF16 CUDA tensors with hidden=512, 1D weight=512, and eps exactly 1e-5; anything else raises NotImplementedError so the outer wrapper falls back to native. Portability note: the fusion is pure portable pointwise/broadcast arithmetic in Triton with no NVIDIA-specific instructions (no tcgen05/TMA/PTX/wgmma); the enable_fp_fusion=False request is the only hardware-dependent knob and is optional. No speed claim is made — this candidate targets exactness parity first; any latency benefit must be established by the independent timed evaluator.
risks: Vendor Triton 2.1.0 may not accept the enable_fp_fusion launch kwarg; handled by a TypeError fallback, but if a backend silently applies FMA elsewhere the per-stage single-product shape (plus the intervening BF16 cast) still prevents cross-stage fusion, so rounding should remain native — this is argued, not independently proven on BI-V150.

Bitwise forward equality is asserted from an external probe on the three given shapes ([128,2,512]); other leading-dimension layouts or strides are only covered because the input is forced contiguous, which could in principle differ if the evaluator feeds shapes the probe did not cover.

Backward is native-equivalent by construction (same op order/dtype) but is NOT fused; if the native C++ backward uses a different internal accumulation order for the mean/pow branch, exactness there relies on Torch's own autograd of the untouched reduction graph rather than on this Function.

sum_to_size is used to reproduce the native reduction targets for g_rstd and g_weight; if an evaluator shape makes weight or rstd broadcasting ambiguous this could mis-reduce, though for hidden=512/weight=512 it is deterministic.
No performance claim is made; the kernel may be slower than native for small [256,512] workloads, and the independent timed gates may still reject the candidate on latency grounds.
Guards reject eps != 1e-5 and non-BF16/non-CUDA/non-512 cases via NotImplementedError; if the outer wrapper lacks a native fallback those cases would error instead of degrading gracefully.
